units.title: Unit 65 — Apologies, excuses and thanks
units.source: English Vocabulary in Use — Pre-intermediate and Intermediate (4th Edition); printed pages 136–137 (PDF pages 137–138).
units.bookTitle: English Vocabulary in Use — Pre-intermediate and Intermediate (4th Edition)
learningObjectives: Choose suitable apologies and reassuring replies in everyday and formal situations.
Distinguish stronger apologies, interruptions and explanations for being late.
Use reasons for delays, cancellations and oversleeping in natural contexts.
Thank someone and answer thanks with an appropriate level of formality.
Apply the apology + for + noun or -ing construction accurately.

items.example: I need to apologise for my mistake.
items.note: British spelling. To say sorry for something you did.

items.example: The manager offered a sincere apology.
items.note: A noun; plural: apologies.

items.example: I'm sorry; I left your keys at home.
items.note: A common apology suitable for many everyday situations.

items.example: I'm really sorry about the mess.
items.note: Really makes the apology stronger and more sincere.

items.example: I'm terribly sorry I damaged your cup.
items.note: Terribly is an intensifier here, not a description of something bad.

items.pt: não tem problema; deixa para lá
items.example: Never mind. We can meet another day.
items.note: A reassuring reply to an apology; it means the mistake is not a problem.

items.example: That's OK. I wasn't waiting long.
items.note: A friendly response to an apology; it can also answer thanks.

items.example: I beg your pardon. I didn't realise you were behind me.
items.note: A more formal apology, especially after accidentally bumping into someone.

items.example: That's all right. Nothing was broken.
items.note: A reassuring reply that accepts an apology.

items.example: Sorry to disturb you. Could I ask a quick question?
items.note: Use before interrupting someone who is busy.

items.example: Don't worry. We still have plenty of time.
items.note: Reassures someone after an apology or concern.

items.example: Come on in. I'm just finishing a message.
items.note: Friendly invitation to enter; often follows an apology for interrupting.

items.example: Sorry to keep you waiting. Your appointment is ready now.
items.note: Use when someone has been waiting for you.

items.example: I won't be long. Please take a seat.
items.note: Promises that someone will only have to wait a short time.

items.example: Excuse me. I need to step outside for a moment.
items.note: Here it is a polite apology before leaving or interrupting, not a request for repetition.

items.pt: volto num instante; não vou demorar
items.example: I won't be a minute. I just need to collect a document.
items.note: Means you expect to return very soon; not necessarily exactly one minute.

items.word: I must apologise for the delay.
items.example: I must apologise for the delay in sending your order.
items.note: A formal apology, particularly useful in letters and professional messages; apologise for + noun or -ing.

items.pt: desculpe pelo atraso; desculpe por chegar tarde
items.example: I'm sorry I'm late. The bus didn't arrive on time.
items.note: Say I’m sorry I’m late, not I’m sorry for be late.

items.pt: pedir desculpas por faltar à reunião
items.example: She called to apologise for missing the meeting.
items.note: Use apologise for followed by an -ing verb to explain an action.

items.example: His excuse for being late didn't sound convincing.
items.note: Noun pronounced /s/ at the end; an explanation for a mistake, which may or may not be true.

items.example: There was a delay because of an electrical fault.
items.note: A delay means that transport or another event happens later than planned.

items.example: A hold-up on the motorway made us late.
items.note: A noun meaning a delay; do not confuse it with the verb phrase be held up.

items.example: We were held up by roadworks.
items.note: Often used in the passive to say something caused a delay.

items.example: I was held up in traffic on the way to work.
items.note: An everyday explanation for arriving late. Compare: there was a delay.

items.example: Our coach was delayed by heavy traffic.
items.note: Passive construction; a close alternative to be held up.

items.example: My train was cancelled because of the strike.
items.note: Cancelled means the service did not run at all, rather than running late.

items.pt: dormiu além da hora; perdeu a hora
items.example: I overslept and missed my morning class.
items.note: Past simple of oversleep; to sleep longer than planned.

items.example: Thanks. You made the problem much easier to solve.
items.note: An informal, common way of expressing gratitude.

items.example: Thanks very much for picking up the parcel.
items.note: Stronger thanks than a simple thanks.

items.example: Thank you for all your help today.
items.note: A polite, widely appropriate way to express gratitude.

items.example: Not at all. I was happy to help.
items.note: A reply to thanks; it does not mean that the help was refused.

items.example: Cheers! I really needed that favour.
items.note: Informal British English for thanks; different from its use in a toast or farewell.

items.example: No problem. Just let me know if you need anything else.
items.note: Informal response to thanks; also a friendly way to accept a request.

items.pt: muita gentileza sua; que gentil da sua parte
items.example: That's very kind of you. I appreciate the offer.
items.note: Polite and slightly more formal thanks for someone's helpful action.

items.example: Could you give my sister a lift to the station?
items.note: British English collocation; a lift is a journey in someone else’s vehicle.

units.title: Unit 66 — Requests, permission and suggestions
units.source: English Vocabulary in Use — Pre-intermediate and Intermediate (4th Edition); printed pages 138–139 (PDF pages 139–140).
units.bookTitle: English Vocabulary in Use — Pre-intermediate and Intermediate (4th Edition)
units.category: Functional language: requests, permission and suggestions
learningObjectives: Make requests with could, possibly, I wonder if, and I was wondering if.
Respond positively and refuse requests politely, using appropriate expressions.
Ask permission using could, may or do you mind if, and interpret their replies.
Suggest activities using how about + -ing, let’s, why don’t we and we could.
Accept or decline a suggestion while expressing preferences accurately.

items.example: Her request was simple and polite.
items.note: A request asks someone to do something; unlike permission, it concerns their action.

items.example: Could you pass me that bottle, please?
items.note: Could you + base verb often expresses a polite request, rather than a question about ability.

items.example: Sure. I can send you the details today.
items.note: Friendly positive reply to a request; informal in many situations.

items.example: No problem. I can print an extra copy for you.
items.note: Positive reply indicating that a request is easy or acceptable.

items.pt: você poderia, por gentileza, me ajudar?
items.example: Could you possibly check these figures for me?
items.note: Possibly makes a request more tentative and polite.

items.example: Yes, of course. You can borrow my notes.
items.note: Warm and confident agreement to a request or permission question.

items.word: I wonder if you could help me.
items.pt: será que você poderia me ajudar?
items.ipa: /aɪ ˈwʌndə ɪf juː kʊd help miː/
items.example: I wonder if you could explain the last step.
items.note: An indirect, polite request; use statement word order after if, not could you.

items.word: I was wondering if you could help me.
items.pt: gostaria de saber se você poderia me ajudar
items.ipa: /aɪ wəz ˈwʌndərɪŋ ɪf juː kʊd help miː/
items.example: I was wondering if you could look at the document tomorrow.
items.note: A particularly tactful indirect request, often used for a larger favour.

items.example: I'm afraid I can't. I'm already busy that evening.
items.note: Polite refusal; afraid expresses regret, not literal fear.

items.example: I'm sorry, but I can't lend you my laptop today.
items.note: Another polite negative reply, usually with a short explanation.

items.example: You need permission to enter this area.
items.note: When asking permission, you ask whether you may do something.

items.word: Could I possibly have a look at that?
items.pt: será que eu poderia dar uma olhada nisso?
items.ipa: /kʊd aɪ ˈpɒsəbli hæv ə lʊk ət ðæt/
items.example: Could I possibly have a look at your timetable?
items.note: Very polite request for permission to examine something.

items.example: Let me have a look at the instructions.
items.note: A common phrase for examining something briefly; use have a look at + noun.

items.example: May I leave a few minutes early?
items.note: May I + base verb is a polite, somewhat formal way to ask permission.

items.example: Could I sit here while I wait?
items.note: Common polite permission question; could can sound less direct than can.

items.word: Do you mind if I sit here?
items.pt: você se importa se eu me sentar aqui?
items.ipa: /duː juː maɪnd ɪf aɪ sɪt hɪə/
items.example: Do you mind if I use this chair?
items.note: A question about whether your action would bother someone. No normally gives permission.

items.example: Help yourself. The biscuits are on the table.
items.note: Gives permission to take or use something without further asking.

items.pt: pode ir em frente; fique à vontade
items.example: Go ahead. You can open the window.
items.note: Gives permission to do the action requested.

items.pt: não, pode fazer; não me importo
items.example: No, go ahead. I don't need the chair.
items.note: A positive answer to Do you mind if…?: no means you do not object.

items.example: That's an interesting suggestion for the weekend.
items.note: An idea offered for someone to consider.

items.pt: o que vamos fazer hoje à noite?
items.example: What shall we do after dinner?
items.note: What shall we + base verb asks for ideas or suggestions.

items.word: We could try that new café.
items.example: We could visit the museum on Sunday.
items.note: We could + base verb offers a possible plan. Do not insert to after could.

items.word: How about going for a walk?
items.example: How about meeting at the station?
items.note: Use how about + noun or -ing form, not how about go.

items.pt: tanto faz para mim; não me importo
items.example: I don't mind. Either restaurant is fine.
items.note: Indicates no strong preference; not an enthusiastic agreement.

items.example: You choose. Both films sound interesting.
items.note: Lets the other person make the decision.

items.example: Let's take the earlier bus.
items.note: Let’s + base verb makes a direct, friendly suggestion.

items.word: Why don't we go for a swim?
items.ipa: /waɪ dəʊnt wiː ɡəʊ fər ə swɪm/
items.example: Why don't we invite Alex as well?
items.note: Why don’t we + base verb is a suggestion, not an ordinary request for a reason.

items.word: Do you fancy going for a walk?
items.pt: você está a fim de dar uma caminhada?
items.ipa: /duː juː ˈfænsi ˈɡəʊɪŋ fər ə wɔːk/
items.example: Do you fancy listening to a podcast later?
items.note: Informal British English. Fancy + -ing asks whether someone wants to do something.

items.example: That's a great idea! We haven't been there before.
items.note: An enthusiastic positive reply to a suggestion.

items.example: That sounds good. What time shall we meet?
items.note: Friendly positive response to an offered plan.

items.example: Yes, if you like. I can come with you.
items.note: Accepts a suggestion without showing a strong preference.

items.example: Yeah, I don't mind. We can eat a little later.
items.note: A relaxed, fairly neutral acceptance.

items.example: I don't fancy that. Could we do something quieter?
items.note: An informal, fairly direct way to decline a proposed activity.

items.example: I'd rather do something else. What about a walk?
items.note: Would rather + base verb states a preference; do not add to.

items.example: I'd rather stay in because I'm tired.
items.note: Used in the practice correction: rather is followed by the base verb, without to.

items.word: Would you like to go out this evening?
items.pt: você gostaria de sair hoje à noite?
items.ipa: /wʊd juː laɪk tə ɡəʊ aʊt ðɪs ˈiːvnɪŋ/
items.example: Would you like to join us for dinner?
items.note: Use Would you like to + base verb to invite someone, not Do you like to for a single invitation.

items.word: What would you like to do?
items.pt: o que você gostaria de fazer?
items.example: What would you like to do on your day off?
items.note: A polite question inviting someone to express a preference.

sectionsChecked: Language help: longer requests and greater politeness
